# 6.7 Asset Allocation

Strategic and tactical allocation; lifecycle allocation and glide paths in practice; international diversification and home bias; rebalancing rules, costs and taxes.

Key file: https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/ai/en/lessons/6.7-key.md

Stage 4 covered the theory of portfolios, capital market assumptions and lifecycle allocation. This lesson turns them into an allocation plan a household can carry out.

## Strategic and tactical allocation

**Strategic asset allocation** is the long-term target mix, for example 60% stocks and 40% bonds. It comes from three things: the household's goals and horizon; the lower of its risk capacity (how large a loss it can bear financially, which depends on human capital, the emergency fund, debts and so on, Lesson 6.6, "The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-6-household-balance-sheet/) and its risk tolerance (how much fluctuation it can bear psychologically); and estimates of the long-run returns and risks of each asset class (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/). The strategic allocation is written into the investment policy statement (IPS) and does not change with short-term market moves.

**Tactical asset allocation** is a temporary departure from the strategic mix based on a view of the short-term market, for example cutting stocks when they look expensive. It is in effect market timing, and like other active management it faces the evidence on market efficiency (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/) and costs (Lesson 6.3, "Active vs. Passive Investing" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-3-active-vs-passive/).

> **Check question C1**
>

>

> (B) Risk tolerance: they can accept a 50% fall, so it can be mainly stocks

## Lifecycle and glide paths

Lesson 4.12, "Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-12-lifecycle-allocation/ showed that if human capital is bond-like, a young person's financial assets can hold more stocks, declining with age. The glide path of a target-date fund standardizes this idea: for example about 90% stocks 40 years before retirement, falling to 40%–50% at retirement. Some funds reach their lowest stock share at the retirement date ("to"), others keep reducing it for some years after retirement ("through").

A particular household's path can depart from the standard: people with stable incomes or pensions can hold more stocks; people whose income moves closely with the stock market (for example in finance or technology, with lots of employer stock) should hold fewer; and large falls in the years just before and after retirement matter most, as Lesson 6.9, "Retirement Planning" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-9-retirement-planning/ discusses.

Following lifecycle allocation, whose financial assets suit a higher stock share?

> (B) The banker, because he understands financial markets
> (C) The same, since their age, wealth and risk aversion are the same
>

## International diversification

By market value, US stocks make up more than 60% of the global stock market (MSCI ACWI Index, 2025), yet US investors often keep most or even all of their stocks in the US; this is called **home bias**. The market portfolio of theory (market portfolio) is global.

Correlations between national stock markets have been fairly high since 2000, so international diversification does little to reduce short-term volatility. Its value shows more over the long run: a single country can go through very long slumps; for example the Nikkei 225's peak of December 1989 was not surpassed until February 2024. Holding foreign assets also brings exchange-rate risk (Lesson 2.7, "The Open Economy" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-7-open-economy/#fx-risk): for stocks, currency moves are a small part of total volatility and are usually left unhedged; for bonds, currency moves can be larger than the bonds' own volatility and are usually hedged (currency hedging). Some common target-date funds hold about 40% of their stocks outside the US.

## Rebalancing

Because assets earn different returns, a portfolio drifts away from its targets. **Rebalancing** means selling assets whose weight is too high and buying those whose weight is too low, bringing the portfolio back to its targets. There are two common rules: rebalance on a calendar (for example once a year), or rebalance when a weight strays more than a set amount from its target (a band rule, for example ±5 percentage points).

> **Check question C4**
> 
> In Figure 4-1, narrow the rebalancing band from ±5 to ±1 percentage point. Which statement is correct?
> 
> (A) The stock weight stays closer to 60%, but rebalancing happens far more often, adding trading costs and taxes
> (B) The narrower the band the better, since risk is controlled more precisely at no extra cost
> (C) The width of the band does not affect how often rebalancing happens
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

Rebalancing has costs too: trading costs, and in taxable accounts capital gains tax on selling appreciated assets (Lesson 6.5, "Accounts and Taxes (US)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-5-accounts-taxes/). In practice these can be reduced: use new contributions, dividends and interest to buy the assets that are underweight; make the adjustments in tax-deferred accounts; trade only when the drift is large.

> **Check question C5**
> 
> A household's stock weight has drifted from its 60% target to 66%. Most of its stocks are in a taxable account with large unrealized gains; its 401(k) holds both stocks and bonds and receives new money every month. The most tax-efficient way to rebalance is:
> 
> (A) Sell stocks and buy bonds inside the 401(k), and direct new contributions to bonds
> (B) Sell stocks in the taxable account, since that is where most stocks are
> (C) No need to rebalance, since rebalancing always creates tax
>
> (Ask it here. The learner only gives an option, without reasons; judge with the key file, and do not give away the answer when it is wrong.)

## Summary

- The strategic allocation is the long-term target mix, set by goals, the lower of risk capacity and tolerance, and capital market assumptions; tactical allocation is short-term timing.
- Glide paths reduce the stock share with age; a particular household should adjust for the nature of its human capital.
- The US is more than 60% of the global stock market; the benefit of international diversification shows mainly over the long run; foreign stocks are usually unhedged and foreign bonds usually hedged.
- Rebalancing brings the portfolio back to its targets, on a calendar or by bands; cash flows and tax-deferred accounts reduce its costs.

## Exercises

Assign them after the lesson. Answers and grading points are in the key file.

**Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)**

A 500,000 dollar portfolio starts the year at 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Over the year stocks rise 30% and bonds fall 5%.
(a) What is the stock weight at year end? How many stocks must be sold to return to 60/40 (thousand dollars)?
(b) A friend says: "Rebalancing sells winners and buys losers, and stocks have momentum (Lesson 4.6, "Multifactor Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-6-multifactor-models/), so rebalancing lowers returns and should be avoided." Evaluate this statement. Consider a simplified example: one asset first rises 50% and then falls by a third (back to its starting price), and the other is cash earning 0; compare holding 50/50 rebalanced each period with starting at 50/50 and never adjusting, and find each one's growth after two periods. What does the example show? In what kind of market does rebalancing earn less?

**Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)**

US stocks have a volatility of 16%, developed markets outside the US 18%, and their correlation is 0.8.
(a) What is the volatility of a stock portfolio of 60% US and 40% international? How much lower than 100% US?
(b) An investor concludes: "International stocks hardly reduce risk and are more volatile, so there is no point in holding them." Evaluate this statement.

**Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)**

An investor's strategic allocation is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. CAPE is now high, and using the building-block method (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/) he estimates stocks will return only 5% a year over the next 10 years, and bonds 4%.
(a) By this estimate, what are the expected returns of 60/40 and 30/70?
(b) He plans to "cut stocks to 30% until valuations come down, then add them back". Evaluate this plan. If his estimate of stocks' expected return really has fallen, what would a reasonable adjustment look like?

**Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)**

A household's portfolio is 1 million dollars with a 60% stock target. Stocks are now 70%, so about 100,000 dollars of stocks must be sold. In their taxable account the stocks' cost basis is only half their market value; the long-term capital gains rate is 15%. Their 401(k) holds 200,000 dollars, all in stocks.
(a) If they sell 100,000 dollars of stocks in the taxable account, how much tax is due (thousand dollars)?
(b) A friend says: "A rule is a rule; every year every account must be put back to 60/40." Evaluate this statement and give a better rebalancing plan.
